title: What pesticide safety training does the EPA Worker Protection Standard require on farms?
description: EPA Worker Protection Standard training under 40 CFR 170.401 and 170.501: annual worker and handler training, trainer rules, topics and 2 year records.
shortAnswer: The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Agricultural Worker Protection Standard at 40 CFR Part 170 requires agricultural employers to train each worker in pesticide safety within the previous 12 months before they work in a recently treated area, and handler employers to train each pesticide handler within the previous 12 months before any handler activity. Training must use EPA-approved materials, a qualified trainer who stays present throughout, and records kept for two years.
keyTakeaways: Worker training under 40 CFR 170.401 is required before any task in a treated area where a pesticide was used, or a restricted-entry interval was in effect, within the last 30 days.
Handler training under 40 CFR 170.501 is required before any handler activity, and both worker and handler training must have been completed within the last 12 months.

Training must use EPA-approved materials, be delivered orally from written materials or audio-visually in a manner workers understand, and be led by a qualified trainer who is present for the entire session and answers questions.
The expanded topic lists (23 topics for workers, those plus 13 more for handlers) apply in place of the original lists, and EPA states that materials with the expanded content must be used.
Records must be kept on the establishment for two years and include the trainee's printed name and signature, date, materials used, trainer name and qualification, and employer name.
regulator: US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), Office of Pesticide Programs, with enforcement by state and tribal pesticide agencies
appliesTo: Agricultural employers on farms, forests, nurseries and greenhouses that produce agricultural plants
Handler employers, including commercial pesticide handler employers and self-employed handlers
Workers who perform tasks directly related to the production of agricultural plants
Handlers who mix, load or apply pesticides, clean or repair application equipment, or assist with applications

sections.heading: Who needs pesticide safety training under the WPS?

blocks.text: Two groups need annual training: workers and handlers. [40 CFR 170.305](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/40/170.305) defines a worker as any person, including a self-employed person, who is employed and performs activities directly relating to the production of agricultural plants on an agricultural establishment. A handler is employed by an agricultural employer or commercial pesticide handler employer and performs handling activities such as mixing, loading or applying pesticides.

Agricultural establishments are farms, forest operations and nurseries engaged in outdoor or enclosed space production of agricultural plants. EPA's [WPS overview](https://www.epa.gov/pesticide-worker-safety/agricultural-worker-protection-standard-wps) describes handlers as those who mix, load or apply agricultural pesticides, clean or repair application equipment, or assist with applications, and workers as those doing tasks such as carrying nursery stock, repotting plants and watering.

Three categories are exempt from worker training under section 170.401(b): workers currently certified as applicators of restricted use pesticides under Part 171, workers who have satisfied handler training under section 170.501, and certified or licensed crop advisors whose program requires training on all handler topics. Handlers certified under Part 171 and qualifying crop advisors are exempt from handler training.

blocks.title: Currency
blocks.text: This page reflects 40 CFR Part 170 as published in the Electronic Code of Federal Regulations as at November 2026. Section 170.501 was last amended at 89 FR 80787 (October 4, 2024), when EPA restored the application exclusion zone provisions of the 2015 rule.

sections.heading: When is worker training due, and what must it cover?

blocks.text: Before any worker performs any task in a treated area where, within the last 30 days, a pesticide product has been used or a restricted-entry interval has been in effect, the agricultural employer must ensure the worker was trained within the last 12 months. The trigger is in [40 CFR 170.401(a)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/40/170.401).

Section 170.401(c)(3) lists 23 topics that replaced the original 11. They include the employer's duties to provide information and protections, recognizing posted warning signs, keeping out of treated areas and application exclusion zones, sources of exposure including drift and irrigation water, routes of entry, signs and symptoms of poisoning, decontamination and eye flushing, emergency medical care, safety data sheets, the prohibition on untrained workers mixing, loading or applying pesticides, the minimum age of 18 for early-entry activities, hazards to children and pregnant women, how to report suspected violations, and the prohibition on retaliation.

The regulation tied the switch to 180 days after EPA published a notice of availability of new training materials, but no earlier than January 1, 2018. EPA's WPS page now states that pesticide safety training materials with the expanded content required by the 2015 WPS must be used to train workers and handlers.

Separately, section 170.403 requires the employer to tell each worker, in a manner they understand, where to find the pesticide safety information, the application and hazard information, and the decontamination supplies on that establishment. That orientation is site specific and sits outside the annual training.

sections.heading: What extra training do pesticide handlers need?

blocks.text: Handlers need all 23 worker topics plus 13 handler topics. Under [40 CFR 170.501(c)(3)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/40/170.501), the additional topics cover proper application and use, following the labeling, the format and meaning of label information, use and removal of personal protective equipment, heat-related illness, safe handling, transport, storage, disposal and spill cleanup, environmental concerns such as drift and runoff, and not applying pesticides in a way that contacts workers or other persons.

Three of the handler topics carry hard rules. Handlers must suspend an application if workers or other persons are in the application exclusion zone and must not resume while they remain, subject to a narrow exception for the owner's immediate family inside closed buildings. Handlers must be at least 18 years old. Handler employers must ensure respirator fit testing, training and medical evaluation when product labeling requires a respirator.

Section 170.503 adds a pre-task duty: before any handler activity, the handler must have read the applicable labeling or been informed of its requirements in a manner they understand, must have access to the labeling throughout, and must be aware of applicable entry restrictions, application exclusion zones and restricted-entry intervals.

sections.heading: How must WPS training be delivered, and who can deliver it?

blocks.text: Training must be presented either orally from written materials or audio-visually, at a location reasonably free from distraction, using EPA-approved materials, in a manner the trainees can understand, such as through a translator. The trainer must be present during the entire program and must respond to questions.

A worker trainer must meet one of three criteria in section 170.401(c)(4): designated as a trainer of certified applicators, handlers or workers by EPA or the state or tribal pesticide agency; completion of an EPA-approved train-the-trainer program for trainers of workers; or current certification as a restricted use pesticide applicator under Part 171. Handler trainers have parallel criteria in section 170.501(c)(4), with the train-the-trainer program for trainers of handlers.

The presence requirement rules out unattended video or self-paced modules as the sole delivery. A video may be used, but the qualified trainer must be in the room, or otherwise present throughout, to take questions. See [eLearning versus instructor-led compliance training](/compare/elearning-vs-instructor-led-compliance-training) for the general trade-offs.

sections.heading: What training records does the WPS require?

blocks.text: Employers must keep a record of each worker's and each handler's training on the agricultural establishment for two years from the date of training. Under sections 170.401(d) and 170.501(d), each record must include the trainee's printed name and signature, the date of training, information identifying which EPA-approved training materials were used, the trainer's name with documentation showing the trainer was qualified at the time, and the employer's name.

An employer who provides the training must give the worker or handler a copy of their record on request. When a worker moves to another establishment, the copy lets a worker prove current training to a new employer within the 12 month window. The guide on [preparing training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit) covers how to keep the five data points complete.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry maps each of the 23 worker topics and 13 handler topics to the concepts and assessment points that show a trainee understood them, so a training session can be checked for full topic coverage before it is delivered. Establishment-specific information is modeled separately, so it is updated when locations change without touching the annual content.

faqs.q: Can a worker trained by a previous employer start work without retraining?
faqs.a: The rule requires the agricultural employer to ensure the worker was trained within the last 12 months, not that the employer delivered the training. A worker can show a copy of a compliant record from another employer. The new employer must still provide the establishment-specific information in section 170.403 before the worker enters a treated area.

faqs.q: Are family farm owners covered by the WPS training rules?
faqs.a: EPA's WPS page states that owners and immediate family members on family-owned farms are exempt from many WPS requirements. Employees on those farms are not covered by the family exemption, so their training obligations remain.

faqs.q: Do certified crop advisors need WPS training?
faqs.a: A crop advisor certified or licensed by a program acknowledged in writing by EPA or the state or tribal pesticide agency is exempt from worker and handler training, provided the certification requires pesticide safety training covering all the handler topics in section 170.501(c)(2) or (c)(3).

faqs.q: What is the application exclusion zone and why is it in training?
faqs.a: EPA describes the application exclusion zone as an area around outdoor application equipment, with a 25 foot or 100 foot radius depending on application type and droplet size, where people are prohibited during application. EPA restored these provisions in 2024, and both worker and handler training topics address staying out of it and suspending applications.
